title: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
summary: How PostgreSQL keeps row versions and snapshots so readers never block writers, what Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable really guarantee, and what versions cost in VACUUM and XID freezing.
outcomes: Decide whether a tuple is visible from its xmin, xmax and a snapshot written as xmin:xmax:xip_list
Explain how Read Committed and Repeatable Read differ in snapshot timing and in concurrent updates
Spot lost updates and write skew in transaction code and choose a fix: atomic UPDATE, FOR UPDATE, or Serializable
Explain how SSI detects dangerous structures of rw edges and why applications must retry on SQLSTATE 40001
Compute how much bloat a long-lived snapshot pins and explain why VACUUM must freeze tuples

lessons.title: Why a database keeps old copies of rows

blocks.md:
Picture a bank database. A report sums every account balance and takes 80 ms. Meanwhile a transfer moves 100 from account A to account B. If the report reads A before the transfer and B after it, the total is off by 100 even though no money was created. The report needs a *consistent* view: every row as of one moment.

A **transaction** is a group of reads and writes that should act as one unit. **Isolation** is the property that concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work.

The classic fix is locking. Readers take shared locks, writers take exclusive locks, and a writer must wait until every reader of that row lets go. It is correct, but a long reader now stalls every writer it touches, and a writer stalls every reader.

**Multiversion concurrency control (MVCC)** takes a different route: an update does not overwrite the row. It writes a *new version* and leaves the old one in place. A reader that started earlier keeps reading the old version; the writer never waits for it.

blocks.title: An 80 ms report and a 10 ms transfer, with and without MVCC

scenes.caption: Simplified locking model: the report holds shared locks from 0 to 80 ms. The transfer arrives at 10 ms, needs an exclusive lock and waits 70 ms, finishing at 90 ms.
With MVCC the transfer writes new versions at 10 to 20 ms and commits. The report keeps reading the old versions, so neither waits and the report still sees one consistent moment.

blocks.md: The PostgreSQL docs state the payoff directly: under MVCC, locks taken for reading do not conflict with locks taken for writing, so *reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading*. Writers still conflict with other writers of the same row; MVCC removes only the reader versus writer conflict.

How does PostgreSQL store the versions? Every row version (a **tuple**) sits in a heap page, which is usually 8 kB. Its 23-byte header holds two transaction IDs:

- `xmin`: the ID of the transaction that inserted this version.
- `xmax`: the ID of the transaction that deleted or replaced it, or 0 if none has.

An UPDATE is in effect a delete plus an insert: it sets `xmax` on the old tuple and writes a new tuple with a new `xmin`. The header field `t_ctid` on the old tuple points to its newer version, forming a chain.

blocks.title: One row, several versions on a heap page

scenes.caption: Transaction 100 inserted account A with balance 500 and committed. One tuple, xmax 0 means nobody has deleted it.
Transaction 105 runs UPDATE balance = 400. It stamps xmax = 105 on the old tuple and writes a new tuple with xmin = 105. Both versions now exist side by side.
A reader whose view predates 105's commit still picks slot 0 (500). A reader that starts after 105 commits picks slot 1 (400). Same row, different answers, no waiting.
Transaction 107 updates again to 450. Slot 0 is now dead to anyone who starts later, but it stays on the page until VACUUM proves no transaction can still see it (lesson 6).

blocks.md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the table itself. The SSI paper by Ports and Grittner notes this differs from designs such as Oracle's, which update rows in place and keep the old values in a separate rollback log. Either way the idea is the same: a reader can reconstruct the row as it was at an earlier moment.
MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

blocks.question: Under PostgreSQL MVCC, transaction W runs UPDATE on row R and has not committed yet. Transaction X now runs UPDATE on the same row R. What happens to X?
options: X proceeds immediately and writes its own version next to W's
X waits until W commits or rolls back
X reads W's uncommitted value and overwrites it
X fails instantly with a serialization error
blocks.explain: MVCC removes reader versus writer blocking only. Two writers on the same row still conflict, so X waits for W to finish. What X does afterward depends on the isolation level, which lesson 3 covers.

blocks.question: A table has 1 row that has been updated 3 times since it was inserted, and no VACUUM has run. How many tuples for that row are on disk?
blocks.explain: The insert created one tuple and each of the 3 updates wrote another, so there are 4 tuples. Only the newest has xmax = 0; the other 3 wait for VACUUM.

lessons.title: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version

blocks.md:
Every tuple carries `xmin` and `xmax`. To decide which versions to show, a transaction needs to know which other transactions count as *already happened* from its point of view. That knowledge is a **snapshot**.

Transaction IDs (**XIDs**) come from one global 32-bit counter. PostgreSQL assigns one lazily, when a transaction first writes, so a read-only transaction may never get one. Commit or abort status for each XID is recorded in the `pg_xact` directory.

A PostgreSQL snapshot has three parts, printed as `xmin:xmax:xip_list`:

- `xmin`: the lowest XID still running. Every XID below it has finished (committed or aborted).
- `xmax`: one past the highest finished XID. Every XID at or above it had not finished, so it is invisible.
- `xip_list`: the XIDs between the two that were still in progress.

The docs' example `10:20:10,14,15` means xmin 10, xmax 20, with 10, 14 and 15 in progress.

The rule then has two halves. A tuple is visible when its **inserter** counts as committed for this snapshot, and its **deleter** does not. An XID counts as committed for the snapshot when it is below `xmax`, not in `xip_list`, and `pg_xact` says it committed. A transaction also sees its own inserts and not its own deletes.

blocks.caption: Simplified from HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC in PostgreSQL's heapam_visibility.c. The real code also handles subtransactions, command IDs within a transaction, frozen tuples and hint bits.
blocks.code:
def finished_and_committed(xid, snap):
    if xid >= snap.xmax:        # not finished at snapshot
        return False
    if xid in snap.xip:         # still running at snapshot time
        return False
    return status[xid] == "committed"  # done: committed or aborted

def visible(t, snap, me):
    if t.xmin == me:            # my own insert
        created = True
    else:
        created = finished_and_committed(t.xmin, snap)
    if not created:
        return False
    if t.xmax == 0:             # never deleted
        return True
    if t.xmax == me:            # I deleted it myself
        return False
    return not finished_and_committed(t.xmax, snap)

blocks.md: Now a worked example. Our snapshot is `100:104:100,102`. Status in `pg_xact`: 99 and 101 committed, 103 aborted, 100 and 102 still running at snapshot time, and 104 committed later, after the snapshot was taken. We are a read-only query with no XID of our own. Below are 8 tuples; work out which ones we see.

scenes.caption: Eight tuples. Inserters 99 and 101 are below xmax, not in the in-progress list, and committed. 102 is in the list, 103 aborted, 104 is at or above xmax.
v1 and v3: committed inserter, never deleted, so visible. v2: inserted by 99 but deleted by 101, which committed before our snapshot, so hidden.
v4: the deleter 102 was still running when we took the snapshot, so its delete does not count for us. We still see v4, even if 102 has committed since.
v5 (inserter 102 in progress), v6 (inserter 103 aborted) and v7 (inserter 104 at or above xmax) all fail the inserter test: hidden.
v8: inserted by committed 101; its deleter 103 aborted, so the delete never happened. Visible. Final answer: v1, v3, v4 and v8.

blocks.title: Tracing visible() for v4 and v8
blocks.code:
def finished_and_committed(xid, snap):
    if xid >= snap.xmax:        # not finished at snapshot
        return False
    if xid in snap.xip:         # still running at snapshot time
        return False
    return status[xid] == "committed"  # done: committed or aborted

def visible(t, snap, me):
    if t.xmin == me:            # my own insert
        created = True
    else:
        created = finished_and_committed(t.xmin, snap)
    if not created:
        return False
    if t.xmax == 0:             # never deleted
        return True
    if t.xmax == me:            # I deleted it myself
        return False
    return not finished_and_committed(t.xmax, snap)

scenes.caption: v4 has xmin 99, xmax 102. We have no XID, so me is None and the first branch is skipped.
99 is below xmax 104 and not in xip, and pg_xact says committed. The tuple was created as far as we are concerned.
The tuple has a deleter, 102. Since 102 is in xip, finished_and_committed returns False, so the delete is invisible and visible() returns True.
v8 has xmin 101, xmax 103. 101 passes. 103 is below 104 and not in xip, but its status is aborted, so the delete does not count.

blocks.prompt: A second query takes its snapshot after 102 commits, while 104 has still not committed and nothing else has changed. Which of v4 and v5 does it see?
blocks.reveal: It sees **v5 but not v4**. The new snapshot is `100:104:100` (only 100 is still running). Now 102 counts as committed: v5's inserter is visible, and v4's deleter is visible, so v4 disappears. Nothing on the page changed; only the snapshot did. This is exactly the lever that isolation levels pull in the next lesson.

blocks.md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.
You can watch this live: `SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts;` shows the system columns, and `SELECT pg_current_snapshot();` prints your snapshot in the `xmin:xmax:xip_list` form.

blocks.question: Snapshot is 200:210:203,207. A tuple has xmin 205 (committed) and xmax 207 (committed after the snapshot was taken). Is it visible?
options: No, because 207 committed
No, because 205 is above the snapshot xmin
Yes, because 207 was in progress at snapshot time so its delete is not seen
Yes, but only if the reader is 207 itself
blocks.explain: 205 is below xmax 210, not in xip and committed, so the insert counts. 207 is in xip, so its delete is invisible to this snapshot regardless of what happened later. Being above snapshot xmin (200) does not matter; only xmax and xip decide.

blocks.question: Why does a tuple with xmin 104 count as invisible for snapshot 100:104:100,102 even though 104 has since committed?
options: Because 104 is greater than or equal to the snapshot xmax, so it had not finished when the snapshot was taken
Because 104 is not in pg_xact yet
Because aborted and committed are treated the same
Because the reader has no XID
blocks.explain: Snapshot xmax is one past the highest finished XID. Anything at or above it was still running or not yet started when the snapshot was taken, so its work is invisible for the life of that snapshot.

lessons.title: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken

blocks.md:
The SQL standard defines four isolation levels by which **phenomena** they forbid:

- **Dirty read**: reading data written by a concurrent transaction that has not committed.
- **Nonrepeatable read**: re-reading a row and finding another transaction changed it and committed in between.
- **Phantom read**: re-running a search and finding a different *set* of matching rows.
- **Serialization anomaly**: a committed result that matches no one-at-a-time order of the transactions.

PostgreSQL implements three distinct levels. Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed; the docs call this the only sensible mapping onto MVCC, where every read goes through a snapshot. Repeatable Read is stronger than the standard demands: it also blocks phantoms. Only Serializable blocks serialization anomalies.

The difference between Read Committed and Repeatable Read is just *when the snapshot is taken*:

- **Read Committed** (the PostgreSQL default): a fresh snapshot at the start of **each statement**.
- **Repeatable Read**: one snapshot at the first statement of the **transaction**, reused until commit.

blocks.title: A nonrepeatable read under Read Committed

scenes.caption: T1 starts and reads account A. Its statement snapshot sees balance 500.
T2 withdraws 100 and commits. Under MVCC this did not wait for T1 and T1 did not wait for it.
Read Committed: T1's second SELECT takes a new snapshot, which includes T2's commit, so it now sees 400. Same transaction, same query, different answer.
Under Repeatable Read, T1 would reuse snap 1 for the second SELECT and see 500 again: a stable view of the database until T1 commits.

blocks.md: Reads are the easy part. The hard part is two transactions **writing** the same row. Recall the **lost update** from Berenson et al.: x = 100, T1 reads 100, T2 reads 100 and writes 120 (+20) and commits, then T1 writes 130 (+30) from its stale read. Final x is 130; any serial order would give 150. T2's update is lost.

PostgreSQL's two lower levels handle a write to an already-changed row differently.

**Read Committed:** the UPDATE waits for the other writer, then, if it committed, re-reads the *newest* version of that row, re-checks the WHERE clause and applies itself to that version. So `UPDATE ... SET x = x + 30` gives 150. But if the application read x into a variable earlier and writes `SET x = 130`, the database cannot know, and 130 wins.

**Repeatable Read:** if the row was changed by a transaction that committed after our snapshot, our UPDATE fails with `could not serialize access due to concurrent update` (SQLSTATE 40001). The application must retry the whole transaction, which then starts from a snapshot that includes 120.

blocks.title: Final x after T1 (+30) and T2 (+20) race, starting from 100

scenes.caption: Any serial order adds both increments: 100 + 20 + 30 = 150. This is the correct answer.
Read Committed with read-then-write in the application: T1 writes the 130 it computed from a stale 100. T2's +20 is lost.
Read Committed with the increment inside the UPDATE: T1 waits for T2, then re-applies x + 30 to the new version 120, giving 150.
Repeatable Read: T1's write fails with 40001 because x changed after its snapshot. The retry reads 120 and writes 150. Correct, at the price of a retry.

blocks.md: Read Committed's re-check can surprise you. The PostgreSQL docs give this case: table `website` has two rows with `hits` 9 and 10. One session runs `UPDATE website SET hits = hits + 1`; concurrently another runs `DELETE FROM website WHERE hits = 10`.

blocks.prompt: Under Read Committed, how many rows does the DELETE remove? For comparison, running the two statements one after the other in either order deletes exactly one row.
blocks.reveal: **Zero.** The DELETE's snapshot sees 9 and 10. Row 9 does not match, so it is skipped. Row 10 matches but is locked by the UPDATE; the DELETE waits, then re-checks the *new* version, which is now 11, and skips it too. The final table is 10 and 11. Serial orders give either one row with 10 (DELETE first) or one row with 11 (UPDATE first). Read Committed produced a result that no serial order produces.

blocks.md: Read Committed is not a weaker form of a single consistent view. Each statement sees one snapshot, but an updating statement can also see newer versions of the rows it is about to change, so a single UPDATE or DELETE can mix two moments in time. The docs call it unsuitable for commands with complex search conditions.

Read Committed: new snapshot per statement, writers re-apply on top of concurrent commits. Repeatable Read: one snapshot per transaction, writers that hit a concurrent commit get error 40001 and must retry.

blocks.question: Your app does `SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id = 7`, computes stock minus 1 in code, then `UPDATE items SET stock = <computed>` in the same Read Committed transaction. Two requests run this concurrently on stock = 5. What can happen?
options: Both requests block forever in a deadlock
Final stock is 3, because Read Committed serializes the updates
The second UPDATE fails with error 40001
Final stock is 4: one decrement is lost
blocks.explain: Both SELECTs can see 5, both compute 4. The second UPDATE waits for the first, then writes the constant 4 onto the new version. Fixes: write `SET stock = stock - 1`, lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or use Repeatable Read and retry on 40001.

blocks.question: A Repeatable Read transaction only runs plain SELECT statements (no FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE). Can it fail with a serialization error in PostgreSQL?
options: Yes, whenever another transaction updates a row it read
No, the docs say read-only Repeatable Read transactions never have serialization conflicts
Yes, if it reads more than one table
Only if it runs longer than the statement timeout
blocks.explain: The 40001 at Repeatable Read comes from trying to modify or lock a row changed after the snapshot. A transaction that only reads never does that, so it never needs a retry at this level.

lessons.title: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through

blocks.md: PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is an implementation of **snapshot isolation (SI)**, a level formalized by Berenson, Bernstein, Gray and colleagues in 1995. Under SI each transaction reads from the snapshot at its start, and a transaction may commit only if no concurrent transaction that committed first wrote the same data (they call this **first-committer-wins**). That prevents dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads and lost updates, and in PostgreSQL also phantom reads.

So is SI serializable? No. Its reads happen at one instant and its writes at another, and the write-write check only looks at transactions writing the *same* row. Two transactions that each read the same data and then write *different* rows never trip it. Berenson et al. name this **write skew** (anomaly A5B): $r_1[x] \ldots r_2[y] \ldots w_1[y] \ldots w_2[x]$, with both committing.

The standard example, from Cahill et al. and repeated by Ports and Grittner: a hospital rule says at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call and both feel ill. Each runs the same transaction: count doctors on call; if the count is at least 2, take *myself* off call. Run alone, either order leaves one doctor on call.

blocks.title: Write skew: both doctors go off call

scenes.caption: Both transactions start under Repeatable Read and count on-call doctors from their own snapshots. Each sees 2.
2 is at least 2, so each updates a different row: Alice's row and Bob's row. No row is written by both, so there is no write conflict and no waiting.
First-committer-wins only checks overlapping writes. There are none, so both commit. Nobody is on call: an invariant that each transaction kept alone is broken.

blocks.md: The PostgreSQL docs give the same shape with sums. Table `mytab` has class 1 rows with values 10 and 20, and class 2 rows with 100 and 200. Transaction A computes `SUM(value) WHERE class = 1` and inserts the result as a new class 2 row. Transaction B computes the class 2 sum and inserts it as a new class 1 row.

blocks.prompt: Under Repeatable Read, both run concurrently and commit. What do A and B insert, and could any serial order have produced that?
blocks.reveal: A inserts **30** (10 + 20) and B inserts **300** (100 + 200). If A had run first, B would have summed 100 + 200 + 30 = **330**. If B had run first, A would have summed 10 + 20 + 300 = **330**. Neither serial order yields the pair (30, 300), so this is a serialization anomaly, even though no row was written twice.

blocks.md: Write skew needs a pattern: each transaction **reads something the other one writes**, and neither writes what the other writes. In serializability theory that is a **read-write antidependency** (rw-conflict): if T1 reads a version of an object and T2 writes the next version, T1 must come before T2 in any equivalent serial order, because T1 did not see T2's write. In the doctors case T1 must precede T2 *and* T2 must precede T1: a cycle, so no serial order exists.

Fekete and colleagues showed even a **read-only** transaction can take part in an SI anomaly. Ports and Grittner's batch example: T3 increments the current batch number, T2 inserts a receipt tagged with the batch number it read (the old one), and T1, a read-only report, reads the new batch number and totals the previous batch. If T3 commits before T1 starts but T2 commits later, the report misses T2's receipt. Without T1, the history is serializable.

Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL is not serializable. The docs warn that business rules enforced by transactions at this level are not likely to work correctly without explicit locks or the Serializable level.
Snapshot isolation prevents conflicts between writes to the same row. Write skew slips through because the conflicting pair is a read and a write to *different* rows.

blocks.question: Which change makes the doctors example safe while staying at Repeatable Read?
options: Run both transactions with a shorter timeout
Add an index on the on_call column
Lock the rows being counted, for example SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on all on-call doctors, so the second transaction waits and then fails or sees the change
Switch to Read Committed so each statement sees fresh data
blocks.explain: Write skew comes from reads that do not conflict with the other transaction's write. Turning the reads into row locks (FOR UPDATE) materializes the conflict: the second transaction blocks, then hits a concurrent update error at Repeatable Read. Read Committed does not help; both counts can still run before either update.

blocks.question: T1 reads x and y, then writes x. T2 reads x and y, then writes x. Both run concurrently under PostgreSQL Repeatable Read. Is this write skew?
options: No: both write x, so the second to write fails or waits, and one gets error 40001 if the first commits
Yes: they read the same data and write after reading
Yes, but only if x and y are in different tables
No, because Repeatable Read blocks all concurrent reads of x
blocks.explain: Write skew requires disjoint write sets. Here both write x, which SI forbids. PostgreSQL enforces this as first-updater-wins: the later writer waits and then fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update.

lessons.title: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures

blocks.md: PostgreSQL's Serializable level (since version 9.1) uses **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, introduced by Cahill, Röhm and Fekete in 2008 and implemented in PostgreSQL by Ports and Grittner. The docs put it simply: it works exactly like Repeatable Read, plus it monitors for conditions that could make the result differ from every serial order, and aborts a transaction when it finds one.

Recall the three dependency edges in a serialization graph, one node per transaction:

- **wr**: T1 writes a version, T2 reads it. T1 must come first.
- **ww**: T1 writes a version, T2 overwrites it. T1 must come first.
- **rw** (antidependency): T1 reads a version, T2 writes the next one. T1 must come first, because it did not see T2.

A non-serializable execution is exactly a cycle in this graph. Under SI, wr and ww edges only run from a transaction that committed before the other started, so the troublemakers are rw edges between *concurrent* transactions.

Fekete et al. proved the key theorem: **every cycle under SI contains two adjacent rw edges** $T_1 \xrightarrow{rw} T_2 \xrightarrow{rw} T_3$, and $T_3$ is the first transaction in the cycle to commit. $T_1$ and $T_3$ may be the same transaction. SSI therefore does not search for cycles. It watches for this **dangerous structure**, a transaction with both an incoming and an outgoing rw edge, which is far cheaper to check.

blocks.title: Dangerous structures in the doctors and batch examples

scenes.caption: Doctors: Alice's T1 read Bob's row, which Bob's T2 then wrote. T1 did not see that write, so T1 must precede T2: an rw edge.
Symmetrically, T2 read Alice's row, which T1 wrote: T2 must precede T1. Two adjacent rw edges form a cycle; here T1 and T3 are the same transaction.
Batch example: T1 is the read-only REPORT, T2 is NEW-RECEIPT, T3 is CLOSE-BATCH. T1 missed T2's receipt (rw); T2 read the batch number T3 then changed (rw).
T1 read T3's new batch number, a wr edge back to T1, closing the cycle. T3 committed first, as the theorem requires. SSI would abort one transaction, preferring T2.

blocks.md: How does PostgreSQL see an rw edge at runtime? Reads under Serializable take **SIRead locks** (shown in `pg_locks` with mode `SIReadLock`) on what they actually accessed: tuples, pages or whole relations. They never block anyone and cannot cause deadlocks. When a later write touches something covered by a concurrent transaction's SIRead lock, PostgreSQL records an rw edge. If the write happened first, the conflict shows up in the MVCC data instead: the reader's visibility check skips a version created by a transaction that had not committed at snapshot time. SIRead locks must outlive their transaction until every overlapping transaction finishes.

When a dangerous structure appears, Ports and Grittner's **safe retry** rules choose a victim. Wait until $T_3$ commits, then abort $T_2$ if possible, since after $T_3$ has committed a retried $T_2$ is no longer concurrent with it and cannot form the same edge. Only if $T_2$ and $T_3$ both committed is $T_1$ aborted. The client sees `could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`, SQLSTATE 40001.

SSI has **false positives**. Not every dangerous structure is part of a real cycle, so some aborted transactions would have been fine. The paper reports serialization failure rates well under 1% on its benchmarks and an overall cost under 7% versus plain snapshot isolation, but your workload may differ.

blocks.caption: A generic retry wrapper with psycopg 3. The whole function reruns, including every read that fed a decision, as the PostgreSQL docs require.

blocks.md:
Practical rules from the docs:

- Declare transactions `READ ONLY` when possible. A read-only transaction can often prove at start that it cannot be part of an anomaly and skip SIRead locks.
- For long reports, `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` waits for a **safe snapshot**, then runs without SIRead locks and can never be aborted.
- A sequential scan takes a relation-level SIRead lock, which raises false positives; index scans lock less.
- When lock memory runs short, fine locks are combined into coarser ones and failures rise. The limits are `max_pred_locks_per_transaction`, `max_pred_locks_per_relation` and `max_pred_locks_per_page`.
- Do not trust data read in a transaction that later aborted.

SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

blocks.question: Two Serializable transactions each run SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id = <own id> on a table with no index on id, then UPDATE their own, different row. PostgreSQL aborts one even though no serial order would differ. Why?
options: SSI blocked on an SIRead lock and the lock timed out
A deadlock between the two updates
Read Committed was used by mistake
A false positive: each sequential scan took a relation-level SIRead lock, so each update formed an rw edge with the other's read
blocks.explain: SIRead locks never block, so there is no timeout or deadlock. Without an index the SELECT uses a sequential scan, which locks the whole relation, so the other transaction's update of a different row still looks like an rw conflict. Edges both ways form a dangerous structure even though neither read cared about the other row. An index on id would avoid it.

blocks.question: In a dangerous structure T1 rw T2 rw T3, T3 has committed and T1 and T2 are still running. Which one does PostgreSQL prefer to abort, and why?
options: T1, because it started first
T2, because once retried it no longer overlaps the committed T3 and cannot form the same structure
T3, by rolling back its commit
None; it waits until all three commit
blocks.explain: Committed transactions cannot be undone. Aborting T1 would leave it concurrent with T2 on retry, so the same structure could reappear. Aborting T2 satisfies the safe retry property.

lessons.title: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound

blocks.md: Old versions cannot stay forever. Once no running transaction's snapshot can see a version, it is **dead**, and its space should be reused. In PostgreSQL that is the job of **VACUUM**, usually run by the **autovacuum** daemon. Plain VACUUM marks dead space reusable but rarely shrinks the file; `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table compactly but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and needs extra disk equal to the table size while it runs.

The catch is the word *can*. A version stays needed as long as **any** snapshot that predates its deletion is alive. A single long-running Repeatable Read report, or a session left idle in a transaction, pins every version deleted after its snapshot was taken.

A simple model: if a table sees $u$ updates per second and the oldest snapshot is $T$ seconds old, about $u \cdot T$ dead versions are unremovable.

blocks.caption: One hour of an open snapshot at 1,000 updates per second. At an assumed 100 bytes per tuple that is about 360 MB of bloat that VACUUM cannot touch until the snapshot ends.

blocks.title: Dead versions pinned by one long-lived snapshot

scenes.caption: Simplified model: every update creates one version that becomes dead but cannot be removed. At 1,000 updates per second, a 60-minute snapshot pins 3.6 million versions.
Double the update rate and the same hour pins 7.2 million. Bloat scales with both rate and snapshot age, so kill idle-in-transaction sessions.
A quiet table at 100 updates per second pins only 0.36 million in an hour. The danger is a busy table plus one forgotten session.

blocks.md: Find the culprit with `pg_stat_activity`: sessions whose `backend_xmin` age is large hold back cleanup. The `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` setting disconnects sessions left idle inside a transaction.

Updates also cost index work: a new tuple normally needs new entries in every index. **Heap-only tuples (HOT)** avoid that when two conditions hold: the update changes no indexed column (BRIN summarizing indexes aside), and the old tuple's page has room for the new version. Then indexes keep pointing at the original item, the chain is followed within the page, and intermediate dead versions can be pruned during normal page access, even by a SELECT, without waiting for VACUUM. Lowering a table's `fillfactor` leaves room for more HOT updates.

VACUUM has a second, non-optional job. XIDs are 32 bits and compared with modulo $2^{32}$ arithmetic: for any XID, about $2^{31}$ (2,147,483,648) XIDs are in the past and $2^{31}$ in the future. A tuple that keeps a normal `xmin` for more than about 2 billion transactions would suddenly appear to be *in the future* and vanish. To prevent this, VACUUM **freezes** old tuples, setting a flag that marks them as older than every normal XID.

blocks.title: How old an unfrozen XID may get (millions of transactions)

scenes.caption: The default autovacuum_freeze_max_age is 200 million. Past that age, autovacuum is forced on the table to freeze it, even if autovacuum is otherwise disabled.
If freezing keeps failing, warnings begin 40 million transactions before wraparound, at an age of about 2,107 million (2^31 minus 40M).
With 3 million left (about 2,144 million), the database refuses commands that assign new XIDs until a VACUUM runs. The wraparound point itself is about 2,147 million.

blocks.md: The same long-running transaction that causes bloat also blocks freezing. The docs' recovery steps for a wraparound emergency are: resolve old prepared transactions, end long-running open transactions, drop stale replication slots, then VACUUM. Raising `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` costs commit-status storage: 2 bits per transaction in `pg_xact`, so 200 million transactions need about 50 MB and the maximum of 2 billion about 500 MB.

blocks.prompt: A 2 TB table only ever receives INSERTs, never UPDATEs or DELETEs. It has no dead tuples. Does it ever need VACUUM?
blocks.reveal: **Yes.** It has no dead space to reclaim, but every row still carries a normal `xmin`. Without freezing, those rows would appear to be in the future after about 2 billion transactions. Autovacuum will force an anti-wraparound vacuum when the table's oldest unfrozen XID passes `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`, and the docs note that this run is not cancelled automatically by conflicting locks. Insert-triggered autovacuum also exists to freeze such tables gradually.

blocks.md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

blocks.question: Autovacuum runs every few minutes on a busy table, yet the table keeps growing and its dead-tuple count never drops. What is the most likely cause?
options: autovacuum_freeze_max_age is set too low
HOT updates are disabled by the fillfactor
A session that opened a transaction hours ago and is still idle in it
The table has too many indexes
blocks.explain: Dead tuples are removable only when no snapshot can see them. An old open transaction holds back that horizon for the whole database, so VACUUM runs but has to keep the versions. End the session and the next VACUUM can clean up.

blocks.question: An UPDATE changes only a non-indexed `last_seen` column, and the page has free space. What does HOT save compared with a normal update?
options: It avoids writing a new tuple version at all
It avoids new index entries, and lets old versions be pruned without VACUUM
It skips writing to the WAL
It makes the update visible to concurrent snapshots
blocks.explain: HOT still writes a new tuple version (MVCC requires it), but on the same page and without new index entries. Intermediate versions can be pruned during normal page access.
